boards.title: Personal Platform Roadmap
boards.description: Cross-repository roadmap for Ryan Laird’s personal platform: portfolio, CV, developer site, documentation, shared content, APIs and supporting infrastructure.
boards.readmeHtml:
Personal Platform Roadmap

A cross-repository roadmap for the platforms that make up my public technical and creative presence.

This project brings together work that spans multiple repositories: the main portfolio site, developer subdomain, CV, documentation, shared content and data, APIs, deployment infrastructure, and the shared components used across the platform.

Rather than tracking every small task in one place, this project focuses on work that affects the platform as a whole: shared data models, reusable components, site architecture, content workflows, deployment, accessibility, performance, and cross-site consistency.

Scope

This project covers:

  • rjmlaird.co.uk — main personal portfolio and public presence
  • dev.rjmlaird.co.uk — developer-focused experiments and technical work
  • cv.rjmlaird.co.uk — CV and professional profile
  • Documentation and content repositories
  • Shared bio, CV, project and contact data
  • Shared UI components, design tokens and navigation
  • APIs, Workers and automation supporting the platform
  • Infrastructure, CI/CD, observability and deployment workflows

What belongs here

Use this project for:

  • Cross-repository features and refactors
  • Shared content, schema and data-model changes
  • Shared UI, navigation and design-system work
  • Platform-wide accessibility, performance and SEO improvements
  • Deployment, domain, API and infrastructure work
  • Major portfolio, CV or documentation releases
  • Work that needs coordination between multiple sites or repositories

What does not belong here

Do not add routine work that belongs entirely to one repository unless it has platform-level significance. Repo-specific bugs, minor content edits and isolated experiments should usually remain in their own repository or project.

How this project is used

  • Now — active cross-platform work
  • Next — agreed upcoming improvements
  • Later — useful but not immediately scheduled
  • Blocked — work waiting on a decision, dependency or external service
  • Done — completed and deployed
  • Archived — no longer relevant or superseded

The aim is a single, calm strategic view of the personal platform: what is being built, what depends on what, and which improvements will have the widest impact.

items.title: [PP-01] Decide canonical host (apex or www) and apply it platform-wide

fields.Title: [PP-01] Decide canonical host (apex or www) and apply it platform-wide

items.bodyHtml:
Context
Open decision #1 in the docs roadmap and the first ADR backlog item. The CV and schema work already use the apex (https://rjmlaird.co.uk/#person) as the canonical identity, while the subdomain inventory proposes apex -> www. It affects every canonical link, sitemap, JSON-LD @id and cookie scope.

Tasks

  • Choose apex or www and record it as an ADR
  • Update SITE_URL / canonical constants in each repo (my-cv src/config/site.ts, master astro config, docs, glossary)
  • Configure the host-level redirect from the non-canonical host
  • Re-run audit:schema (master) and check:live (cv) to confirm @ids and canonicals still agree

Done when: ADR accepted; one canonical host in every sitemap, canonical tag and JSON-LD @id; redirect verified.

items.title: [PP-02] Decide the fate of cv. and dev. subdomains versus /cv and /dev routes

fields.Title: [PP-02] Decide the fate of cv. and dev. subdomains versus /cv and /dev routes

items.bodyHtml:
Context
The sources disagree. The CV repo is a full subdomain deploy that is self-canonical. The main site also has a /cv/ route (the CV checklist warns of two competing copies) and its README calls cv. and dev. 'retired subdomains' that need redirects. The docs inventory recommends merging cv into /cv and deferring dev. This project's scope still lists both. GitHub Pages cannot issue 301s.

Tasks

  • Decide per site: keep as subdomain, or merge into a path on the main site
  • If cv. stays: redirect or canonical the main site's /cv/ to https://cv.rjmlaird.co.uk/
  • If retired: configure redirects on the host serving the subdomain and update sameAs, status services and docs
  • Record the outcome as an ADR and update subdomains.json

Done when: One live home for the CV and the dev workbench; no duplicate pages competing; status page and schema reflect the decision.

items.bodyHtml:
Context
The CV deploy workflow already listens for repository_dispatch (content-updated) plus a 04:17 UTC nightly, but nothing fires it from the API repo. The main site only deploys on push to main and also reads the API at build time, so its content can go stale too.

Tasks

  • Add the dispatch step to the API repo workflow (gh api repos/rjmlaird/my-cv/dispatches)
  • Add repository_dispatch and a nightly schedule to master's deploy.yml
  • Use a fine-grained token scoped to the target repos only
  • Document the contract in docs (automation-workflows)

Done when: Changing API data triggers rebuilds of both sites without a code push.

items.bodyHtml:

Tasks

  • Add axe-core to CI on every built site with agreed page lists
  • Set Lighthouse thresholds (accessibility >= 95, aim 100) and a performance budget
  • Self-host fonts everywhere and tighten CSP headers
  • Run the keyboard and screen-reader checklist on shared components; align the accessibility statement

Done when: CI fails on accessibility regressions on every site; no third-party font requests.

items.bodyHtml:

  • Delete the second lockfile in master and docs; set packageManager
  • Upgrade status and glossary to the supported Astro
  • Adopt the minimumReleaseAge and install-script allow-list policy everywhere; enable Dependabot or Renovate

Done when: All repos share one documented toolchain and one lockfile.

boards.readmeHtml:
AI Workflow Dashboard

A self-hosted dashboard for managing AI-assisted workflows, agent tasks, prompt jobs, and human review.

This project gives me a single place to plan, run, inspect, and improve AI workflows across content, research, automation, and product work.

What it does

  • Tracks AI jobs from request to completion.
  • Manages prompts, templates, and versions.
  • Monitors agent tasks and workflow status.
  • Shows output logs, errors, and review states.
  • Records usage, runtime, and cost signals.
  • Supports human-in-the-loop approval before publishing or actioning results.

Why it exists

AI work becomes hard to manage when it is scattered across notebooks, scripts, chat windows, and automation tools. This dashboard turns that process into something visible, repeatable, and easier to audit.

Core features

  • Workflow queue.
  • Prompt library.
  • Job detail view.
  • Output review panel.
  • Status tags and filters.
  • Metrics and cost tracking.
  • Error and retry handling.
  • History and audit trail.

Suggested stack

  • Astro or Next.js for the UI.
  • React for dashboard components.
  • TypeScript for typed workflow models.
  • Python for backend jobs and automation.
  • PostgreSQL or SQLite for storage.
  • GitHub Actions for scheduled tasks.
  • Zod for schema validation.

Example workflow

  1. Create a new task from a template.
  2. Send it to one or more agents.
  3. Store intermediate outputs and logs.
  4. Review the result manually.
  5. Approve, reject, or rerun.
  6. Publish the final output to another repo or system.

Future ideas

  • RAG support.
  • MCP integrations.
  • Multi-agent routing.
  • Browser or API connectors.
  • Budget alerts and usage caps.
  • Search across past runs.
  • Replay and compare outputs.

Status

Early-stage concept project.

boards.readmeHtml:
Platform Infrastructure

A cross-repository board for the technical foundations behind Ryan Laird’s personal platform and labs.

This project tracks infrastructure, automation and maintenance work that supports multiple sites and repositories. It is concerned with keeping the platform reliable, secure, observable, easy to deploy and inexpensive to operate.

Purpose

The platform includes several independently deployed sites, labs, APIs, Workers and shared packages. This project provides one place to manage the shared technical work that would otherwise be scattered across individual repositories.

It focuses on:

  • Deployment pipelines and release workflows
  • Cloudflare Workers, APIs and serverless functions
  • Shared TypeScript, UI, content and configuration packages
  • CI/CD, testing, linting and type checking
  • Dependency updates and security patching
  • Domain, DNS, routing and environment configuration
  • Monitoring, logging, error tracking and uptime
  • Backups, data retention and disaster recovery
  • Cost, performance and resource efficiency

Scope

This project covers infrastructure affecting:

  • The main portfolio site
  • Developer and CV subdomains
  • Labs deployments
  • APIs and Workers
  • Shared content, UI and configuration packages
  • Automation scripts and GitHub Actions
  • Data pipelines and scheduled jobs

Core workstreams

  • Deployment — consistent build, preview and production deployment workflows
  • Reliability — monitoring, alerting, error handling and recovery
  • Security — dependency updates, secret management, access control and vulnerability response
  • Developer experience — reusable CI templates, local development setup and documentation
  • Shared packages — versioning, publishing, compatibility and upgrade paths
  • Automation — issue syncing, labelling, release notes, scheduled jobs and repetitive maintenance
  • Performance and cost — caching, bundle size, API efficiency and hosting cost control

Operating principles

  • Prefer small, reusable workflows over duplicated CI configuration
  • Keep deployments independent, but standardise shared patterns
  • Make infrastructure changes reversible where possible
  • Document ownership, environment variables, secrets and rollback steps
  • Treat monitoring and backups as essential, not optional
  • Avoid premature complexity: use the simplest reliable solution first

What belongs here

  • Deployment failures and pipeline improvements
  • New Workers, APIs or automation workflows
  • Shared package refactors and version bumps
  • CI/CD, testing and dependency-maintenance work
  • Monitoring, logging and alerting improvements
  • Security, secrets and access-management tasks
  • Infrastructure documentation and runbooks
  • Cost, performance and reliability improvements

This project is the maintenance layer of the platform: the work that keeps individual experiments, sites and services dependable enough to build upon.

boards.readmeHtml:
Content & Publishing

A cross-repository editorial pipeline for writing, science communication, portfolio content, documentation and reusable personal data.

This project tracks content from initial idea through research, drafting, review, publication and repurposing. It covers material intended for the main portfolio site, developer site, CV, documentation, labs and any future publishing surfaces.

Purpose

The purpose of this project is to maintain a clear, repeatable content workflow so that ideas do not get lost and published work remains accurate, discoverable and reusable.

It supports:

  • Essays and long-form writing
  • Science communication and public-facing explanations
  • Technical documentation and project write-ups
  • Portfolio project descriptions and case studies
  • CV, bio, contact and achievement content
  • Content derived from labs, research and data experiments
  • Updates, corrections and archival of published material

Content lifecycle

  1. Idea — capture the topic, audience and intended outcome
  2. Research — gather sources, data, references and examples
  3. Outline — define structure, argument and key messages
  4. Draft — produce the first complete version
  5. Review — check accuracy, clarity, tone, accessibility and links
  6. Ready to publish — final edits, metadata, images and previews complete
  7. Published — live on the relevant site
  8. Repurpose — adapt for social posts, newsletters, documentation or project pages
  9. Archive / update — revisit when facts, links or context change

Content principles

  • Prioritise accuracy, clear sourcing and honest uncertainty
  • Write for a curious but non-specialist audience where appropriate
  • Make technical work understandable without oversimplifying it
  • Keep reusable facts — bio, CV, projects, contact details — in a single source of truth
  • Avoid duplicating the same content across multiple repositories
  • Update or retire content when it becomes outdated

What belongs here

  • Essay and article ideas
  • Drafts, revisions and publication tasks
  • Documentation improvements
  • Portfolio project descriptions
  • CV and profile content updates
  • Content migrations and restructuring
  • Fact-checking, source review and link maintenance
  • Repurposing published work into other formats

This project treats content as part of the platform’s infrastructure: structured, maintained, reusable and designed to remain useful over time.

boards.title: Builds: Labs, Tools & Apps
boards.description: A cross-repository board for Ryan Laird’s builds: experimental labs, practical tools and more complete apps, tracked from initial idea through prototype, publication and maintenance.
boards.readmeHtml:
Builds: Labs, Tools & Apps

A single cross-repository project for tracking the things I build: experiments, utilities, visualisations, dashboards, data pipelines and interactive applications.

Builds are the durable record of a project. Labs, Tools and Apps are not separate project types—they are surfaces or maturity labels that describe how a build is currently presented and used.

This allows one idea to evolve without losing its history:

Idea → Lab experiment → Working demo → Tool → App

For example, a climate or flood dashboard may begin as a Labs experiment, become a Tool once its data pipeline and interface are reliable, and eventually be presented as an App when it is polished, maintained and ready for regular use.

Purpose

This project exists to:

  • Track builds across multiple repositories in one place
  • Make the path from experiment to usable tool or app explicit
  • Avoid duplicating the same project across separate Labs, Tools and Apps boards
  • Preserve a single history of issues, decisions, pull requests and releases
  • Identify which experiments are worth promoting, maintaining or archiving
  • Coordinate shared work such as UI components, metadata, catalogues, APIs and deployment patterns

Surfaces

Each build has one primary surface:

Surface Meaning
Labs Experimental, exploratory or provisional work; prototypes, research spikes, data experiments and interface tests
Tools Practical, reusable utilities designed to solve a specific problem or support a repeatable workflow
Apps More complete, maintained interactive products, dashboards or services intended for ongoing use

A build can change surface as it matures. It should not be duplicated across surfaces; update its classification instead.

Build lifecycle

  1. Idea — identify the question, dataset, need or opportunity
  2. Spike / research — test feasibility, data availability or technical approach
  3. Prototype — build the smallest useful version
  4. Working demo — a functional version that can be shared
  5. Published — publicly available through Labs, Tools or Apps
  6. Maintained — actively improved, documented and kept working
  7. Archived — paused, superseded or no longer maintained

What belongs here

  • New build ideas and research questions
  • Data-source evaluation and pipeline development
  • Prototypes, demos and interface experiments
  • Tools, dashboards, visualisations and interactive applications
  • Improvements to existing builds
  • Promotion decisions between Labs, Tools and Apps
  • Shared catalogue metadata, navigation and UI components
  • Deployment, documentation and maintenance work that affects a build

What does not belong here

Routine work that belongs entirely to one repository and has no broader build or platform significance should normally stay in that repository. General infrastructure, portfolio-site work and content publishing are tracked in their own projects.

Working principles

  • Prefer small, focused builds over large premature platforms
  • Keep independently deployed builds decoupled where practical
  • Document data sources, assumptions, limitations and update frequency
  • Share stable components and patterns, but avoid coupling unfinished experiments too tightly
  • Promote a build only when it has a clear purpose, usable interface and sustainable maintenance path
  • Treat unfinished work as valid: not every experiment needs to become an app

This project is the operational home for my builds: a place to explore ideas publicly, turn useful experiments into practical tools, and develop the strongest ones into maintained applications.

items.title: [BB-01] Unify the three build registries into one Builds catalogue

fields.Title: [BB-01] Unify the three build registries into one Builds catalogue

items.bodyHtml:
Context
Each repo has its own export-builds.ts and registry (labs.ts, tools.ts, apps.ts). Statuses are active / in-progress / planned / archived, but this project's lifecycle has seven stages (Idea to Archived). Ids are prefixed by surface (tools/julian-date), so promoting a build would change its id. The apps registry does not type-check (path?: url), launches is unregistered, and the labs export writes to a sibling ../rjmlaird-api path outside the repo. Labs tech and updated values are hand-maintained.

Tasks

  • Agree one schema: id, surface, stage (lifecycle), group, tech, updated, repository, url, aliases (previous ids)
  • Map today's four statuses to the seven lifecycle stages and record the mapping
  • Fix the apps registry type error and register launches; correct astrodash's tech label (it says Python/Streamlit)
  • Derive tech and updated from a per-build manifest (lab.json or equivalent) instead of editing by hand
  • Make export-builds --check identical in all three repos

Done when: All three exports validate against one schema and contain every build; ids survive a surface change via aliases.

items.title: [BB-02] Decide the URL scheme and redirects when a build changes surface

fields.Title: [BB-02] Decide the URL scheme and redirects when a build changes surface

items.bodyHtml:
Context
Tools are path-based Workers (tools.rjmlaird.co.uk/), apps are one subdomain each (.apps.rjmlaird.co.uk), and labs are described as .labs.rjmlaird.co.uk. This project says a build should change classification rather than be duplicated, which implies its URL moves. Two-level wildcard hostnames may also need an Advanced Certificate on Cloudflare (to confirm). The Platform Roadmap (project 1) already has a decision on whether subdomains are justified (PP-33, ADR-0002).

Tasks

  • Choose one URL pattern per surface and justify any subdomain use against the ADR-0002 test
  • Confirm certificate coverage for any second-level wildcard
  • Define the redirect rule and who owns it when a build is promoted (old URL 301s to new, alias kept in the registry)
  • Record the decision as an ADR in the docs repo

Done when: ADR accepted; a promotion never breaks an existing link.

  • Decide what to store (titles, links, short excerpts and your own entity tags, not full article text) and the copyright position

  • Define the entity taxonomy (launch operators, agencies, programmes, constellations) as shared data
  • Compute the charts from stored data and escape all rendered text
